transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because my concentration just hasn’t been reliable lately. I’ll be at the clinic reviewing a patient chart, or even at home working on a watercolor, and I’ll realize I’ve read the same line over and over while my mind’s off on everything that could go wrong. It’s been getting hard to trust my focus.
Have you been feeling sad or down lately?
I don’t think so, not really. I mean, I get frustrated and worn out by all this, but I wouldn’t describe it as feeling sad or down most of the time.
Have you been feeling anxious or on edge lately?

Yes. I’ve been pretty anxious, and it’s hard to shut off. My mind keeps going around and around about different things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff of the practice makes financial sense, whether I’m going to become useless once I’m fully retired. Even to me, the amount I worry feels bigger than it should.
Have you experienced any panic attacks recently?
I don’t think so. I mean, I get anxious, but I haven’t had anything I’d call a panic attack recently.
Have you been avoiding any activities or situations because of your anxiety?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m avoiding things, exactly. I still do what I need to do. I might hesitate or put something off a bit when I’m anxious, but nothing obvious comes to mind that I’ve stopped doing because of it.
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts that are difficult to control?

Yes. I’ll try to talk myself through it logically, like I would with a nervous patient, but it doesn’t really stop. One concern leads to another, and before I know it I’m checking emails again, looking over notes, or asking the same questions instead of just letting it go.
Do you feel compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors to reduce your anxiety?
I don’t think I have rituals, no. I may double-check something if I’m uneasy, but it’s not like I have a set routine I feel I must do to calm down.
Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to ignore them?

Yes, they do. I try to reason with myself and calm it down, kind of like I would with a nervous patient, but it doesn’t really stop. One worry leads to another, and then I’m back checking emails or going over notes, or asking the same thing again instead of just letting it go.
Do you feel like these repetitive thoughts are unreasonable or excessive?

Yes, I do. I mean, the things I worry about are real enough—my old patients, the practice handoff, money, retirement—but the way my mind keeps going around and around them feels bigger than it should. Even I can tell it’s out of proportion sometimes.
Is there one specific thing that you worry about most of the time, or are your worries spread across many different areas of your life?

It’s spread across a lot of things, really. I worry about whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the practice handoff was financially solid, whether I’m going to become useless once I’m fully retired… it just keeps circling from one thing to the next. And even to me, it feels bigger than it should.
Do you often feel restless or like you're on edge, even when there's no apparent reason for it?
I’m not really sure. I don’t know that I’d call it being restless for no reason. I do feel keyed up at times, but usually I can connect it to something I’m worried about.
Would you say that you worry about most things in your life most of the time?

Yes, I’d say most of the time, it’s there. It isn’t just one thing—my mind keeps moving between my former patients, whether the practice handoff was financially sound, what retirement is going to make of me. Even while I know those are normal things to think about, the amount I worry feels out of proportion.
Is it rare for you to have a day where you don't worry about something?

Yes, it is pretty rare. Most days my mind finds something to latch onto—my old patients, the money side of the handoff, what retirement means for me. It just keeps going around, and even I can tell the amount of worry is more than it needs to be.
Do you worry about everyday, mundane things like what to eat or what to wear?

Not usually things like what to eat or wear, no. It’s more that my mind keeps circling around bigger things—whether my old patients are being looked after, whether the practice handoff was financially sound, and what I’ll be worth once I’m fully retired. Even to me, the amount I worry about it feels out of proportion.
Would you say that your worrying affects almost every area of your life?

Yes, I think it does, maybe not every single area, but more than I’d like to admit. I’ve had to slow down and put off parts of the retirement handoff because I keep second-guessing decisions, and I lose time at the clinic over it. Even things I used to enjoy, like painting and gardening, feel harder to manage than they used to.
Do you have thoughts that are intrusive, meaning they come into your mind without you wanting them to?

Yes, they do. I’ll be trying to move on with my day, and then a concern just pops in—about the practice, or a patient, or the handoff—and I can’t seem to let it sit there. I try to talk myself through it logically, like I would with a nervous patient, but then one worry leads to another. Before I know it, I’m checking emails, looking over notes, or asking the same question again instead of letting it go.
Is your anxiety primarily focused on one area of your life, such as your retirement or the practice handoff, or is it more generalized across many areas?

It started mostly around the practice and retirement, but it doesn’t stay neatly in one box. My mind keeps circling around all sorts of things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff makes financial sense, whether I’ll feel useless once I’m fully retired. And honestly, even to me, the amount I worry about it feels out of proportion.
Would you say that there is one main thing that causes you the most anxiety, or are your anxieties spread out across many different things?

It’s spread out, I’d say. The practice handoff is a big part of it, but then my mind goes to whether my old patients are being looked after, whether the finances make sense, and whether I’ll feel useless once I’m fully retired. It keeps circling, and even I can tell the amount of worry is more than it should be.
Is your anxiety mostly about one or two big things, or is it about a lot of little things all the time?

It’s more about a lot of things, really. The handoff is one of the bigger ones, but my mind keeps jumping to other worries too—whether my old patients are being taken care of, whether the finances are sound, whether I’ll feel useless once I’m fully retired. It just keeps circling, and even I can see it’s more worry than the situation probably calls for.
